title: Zonal ingress mTLS pass-through and firewall staging matrix
content:
Purpose:

This is a working playbook for introducing zonal mTLS pass-through support and a staged firewall rule promotion process for private (VPC/on-prem) Redwood deployments. Goals: allow a controlled rollout where some zones use TLS termination at the ingress controller while others forward TLS to backend pods (pass-through). Provide a clear Terraform upgrade path, verification tests, and rollback steps.

Scope:
- Private deployments (VPC or on-prem clusters) that run Kubernetes managed by our private control plane.
- Ingress traffic (north-south) for customer workloads only — not internal control-plane traffic.
- Firewalls: both cloud/VPC security groups and on-prem perimeter firewalls.
- Network policies (CNI-level) and kube-proxy/conntrack tuning required for high connection churn.

Assumptions and constraints:
- Clusters run either NGINX ingress controller (legacy) or envoy-based ingress (preferred).
- Backends support TLS when pass-through is enabled. Certificate rotation must be in place (Vault or KMS-backed certs).
- Load balancers (LB) support TCP health checks when using pass-through; LB session affinity may be required.
- Terraform modules must remain backward-compatible; feature flags to opt in per-cluster/zone.

High-level plan (stages):
1) Prepare terraform modules (no traffic change)
  - Add opt-in boolean: ingress_tls_passthrough_enabled (default false)
  - Add new resources: lb_tcp_healthcheck, lb_tcp_listener, and enhanced firewall rule objects with "staging" tag/metadata
  - Expose per-zone variable maps so some zones can flip without touching others
2) Deploy infra changes (no flux to apps)
  - Apply TF plan that creates listeners and healthchecks, adds firewall staging rules (shadow mode)
3) Deploy ingress controller config changes to support passthrough (configmap + secret references)
4) Enable pass-through on a small canary zone (zone-a) and run synthetic traffic tests
5) Promote firewall rules (shadow -> active) per-zone after validation
6) Gradual rollout to other zones, monitor, and finalize by pruning legacy termination config

Terraform module notes (developer-facing):
- Module changes (recommended):
  * variables.tf: add map(string) "zone_ingress_mode" default { } where value is "terminate" or "passthrough" per zone
  * variables.tf: add bool "enable_ingress_passthrough" default = false (global guardrail)
  * main.tf: create aws_lb_target_group (tcp) when passthrough enabled, keep existing http/https target groups for termination mode
  * security_group.tf: create security rules with tag "stage:ingress-passthrough" that mirror the final rules but are not attached to critical ACLs until promote step
  * outputs.tf: expose listener_arn and healthcheck_id to the cluster bootstrap module so ingress can reference them
- Backwards compatibility: new resources are created in the same TF apply; they should be additive. Ensure destroy-time ordering keeps termination intact if passthrough is later removed.

Ingress controller configuration differences:
- Termination mode (existing): LB terminates TLS (443), forwards HTTP to ingress controller on port 80/8080.
- Pass-through mode: LB forwards TCP 443 to a target group bound to node ports or directly to pod IPs. In this model:
  * Ingress must mark specific hostnames as TLS passthrough in annotations/CRD.
  * Health checks: TCP or custom TLS-aware checks. HTTP healthchecks will fail if forwarded as TCP.
  * Session affinity: consider "source-ip" affinity to reduce rehandshake load.

Kubernetes annotations / examples (envoy-ingress):
- For passthrough virtualservice: annotations: ingress.kubernetes.io/tls-passthrough: "true"
- For nginx tcp config (when NGINX supports stream): create a ConfigMap tcp-services mapping 443 -> service:8443 with upstream mode: "passthrough"

Private DNS and certificate considerations:
- When using passthrough, backend service certificates must have SANs for the public hostnames or use a wildcard that matches.
- Private DNS split-horizon: ensure the private zone resolves customer hostnames to the LB internal IPs. Avoid TTL juggling mid-rollout; low TTLs (30s) during rollout help, but be mindful of DNS query spikes.
- Recommend: pre-create DNS records pointing to the new TCP listeners in each zone before enabling passthrough.

NAT / connection-tracking implications:
- Pass-through means longer-lived TLS connections to pods; connection churn patterns may change. Increase conntrack_max and tune timeouts on nodes where TLS passthrough is enabled (particularly on on-prem with limited conntrack tables).
- Suggested sysctls for high churn nodes:
  * net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 262144
  * net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established = 86400
  * net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_time_wait = 30
- If using nodePort targeting, ensure external NAT (cloud NAT or firewall) does not SNAT session source IP unless required. If SNAT is in place, session affinity by cookie or LB-side source-ip will be ineffective.

Firewall rule staging matrix (how we promote):
- Strategy: create three states for firewall rules: shadow (log-only), staged (rate-limited allow), active (full allow).
- For each zone and CIDR-range:
  1) Shadow: add an allow rule with logging enabled but no enforcement (cloud vendor: set priority to lower than existing deny, or use monitor-only flag).
  2) Staged: allow rule with strict rate limit (if supported) and short session timeouts; monitor application errors for 24–48 hours.
  3) Active: final allow rule without rate limits and with production idle timeouts.
- Terraform: define firewall_rule resource with argument "mode" = ["shadow","staged","active"]; implement lifecycle create_before_destroy and use a promoted boolean to flip rules in-place via a small state machine script (see linked artifacts).

NetworkPolicy and CNI notes:
- Prefer Cilium for on-host TLS passthrough workloads because of its fast L7-aware policies and ability to do BPF-based redirect. Calico works but requires iptables bridging which can be slower under heavy loads.
- If using ingress passthrough at nodePort level, ensure NetworkPolicies permit nodePort range from LB CIDRs to the pod endpoints.

Test plan (synthetic + production smoke):
- Canary zone tests (zone-a):
  * Synthetic TLS handshake test to backend (openSSL s_client -connect <ip>:443 -servername host) verifying certificate chain and SNI passthrough.
  * Replay production traffic via a traffic replay tool (k6/siege) using sampled request traces.
  * Latency and CPU baseline comparison: measure TLS handshake CPU on pods pre/post.
  * Health-check validation: ensure LB healthchecks succeed against tcp listeners.
- Monitoring metrics to watch: tls_handshakes/sec, handshake_time_ms, pod_cpu_user/limit, conntrack_table_utilization, 5xx spikes in app logs.

Rollback plan:
- If canary fails: flip the zone_ingress_mode for the canary zone back to "terminate" in the cluster config; remove passthrough annotations and restart ingress.
- Terraform rollback: if firewall staging caused reachability issues, revert firewall mode to previous state (shadow/deny) via the promotion script; because we used create_before_destroy lifecycle, revert is low-risk.
- If cert mismatches: switch client-facing hostnames back to LB TLS termination (fast path) and rotate certs for backend.

Runbook snippets (operators):
- Check health of tcp listener (AWS ALB example): aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn $TG_ARN
- Verify passthrough handshake from bastion: openssl s_client -connect 10.10.3.22:443 -servername api.customer.example.com -showcerts
- Observe conntrack on node: sudo conntrack -L | wc -l

Monitoring and alerts:
- Create temporary alerts for rollout window:
  * Alert: conntrack_utilization > 70% for 5m -> paged to SRE channel
  * Alert: tls_handshakes_5xx_rate > 0.5% for 10m -> page dev owner
  * Alert: lb_healthcheck_failures > 1% over 15m -> page infra oncall

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Do we want to prefer nodePort-based passthrough vs direct pod target group in cloud? NodePort reduces LB complexity but increases node egress/NAT surface.
- Should we build an automated TF promotion controller that flips firewall rules via API or keep manual promotion as the default?
- Are all customer workloads capable of handling long-lived TLS connections and SNI-preservation? Need inventory.

Next steps (actionable):
- PR terraform modules (draft) -> @Ethan Park to author initial module changes (TF PR link above).
- Create test cluster in zone-a with passthrough toggled -> @Maya Singh to provision and run synthetic tests.
- Audit active customer certs for SAN coverage -> @Omar Haddad to produce a short report (deadline: 2025-03-14).

Notes to self / rough checklist (quick):
- [ ] Add variable maps for per-zone ingress mode
- [ ] Add listener/healthcheck TF resources (tcp)
- [ ] Create shadow firewall rules with logging
- [ ] Add conntrack sysctl template to cluster bootstrap
- [ ] Prepare synthetic replay harness and baseline metrics
- [ ] Draft a short KB article for customers describing what to expect during the rollout

End of draft.
